reader.title: Threatened lynching of J. A. Hogan
chips: Lynching of any race (not in the anti-Black count)
bases: A mob pursued or seized a man accused of a shooting and threatened to lynch him, then handed him to the sheriff; no one was killed by the mob (A1, A4, A9).
The mob that meant to lynch Hogan for the shooting of Falvey surrendered him to the sheriff instead, so no one was killed by a group (A1, A4); the mob's size is not given.

The shooting and Hogan's capture are confirmed by a local Black Hills account and later Dakota items (A13, A15, A17), but the lynching threat rests on one Deadwood wire dispatch reprinted and reworded across the country (A1, A3, A4, A9); the local account does not mention a mob (A13).

summary.text: The threatened lynching of J. A. Hogan took place at Central City, in the Black Hills of Dakota Territory, on the morning of November 23, 1880, when a mob went after Hogan, who had just shot a miner named Dan Falvey, intending to lynch him.
The mob finally surrendered Hogan to the sheriff, and he was later tried for murder and found guilty of manslaughter after Falvey died.
A Deadwood dispatch carried the episode to papers from Chicago to Los Angeles, some under headlines such as "Almost a Lynching"; none of the reports states the race of anyone involved.
According to a local Black Hills account printed in the Custer Chronicle, Hogan and Falvey both worked the night shift at the "De Sinet" mine and boarded at the Rustic hotel in Central City.
At about 8 a.m., on their way back from work, the two stopped at King's saloon, where they drank and fell into a political argument that continued at the hotel.

In the hotel office, with one or two others present, Hogan drew a pistol; the same account says Falvey apparently tried to take the gun or turn the muzzle aside, and it went off, wounding him in the abdomen.
Hogan tried to escape but was captured and placed in custody to await a preliminary hearing.
The wire version adds that "a mob got after Hogan, intending to lynch him, but finally surrendered him to the Sheriff."
The Chicago Daily Tribune's front-page summary went further, saying the mob "got hold of" Hogan and threatened to lynch him before turning him over to the authorities.
No report names the sheriff or any member of the mob, gives its size, or says where Hogan was caught and handed over.
Falvey died early on Thanksgiving morning, and his funeral the next afternoon was described as one of the largest ever seen in Deadwood.
In January 1881 a Yankton paper reported that John A. Hogan, tried for murder in Lawrence County, had been found guilty of manslaughter; the degree is unreadable in the surviving text.
No report of an inquest or of any action against the mob was found.

The Deadwood dispatch ran on November 24 in the Sacramento Daily Record-Union, the Chicago Daily Tribune, the Daily Los Angeles Herald, the Cheyenne Daily Leader, the Salt Lake Herald, the St. Paul Daily Globe and the Las Vegas Morning Gazette, and later in weekly papers in Arizona and Minnesota.
Headlines framed it as a near-lynching ("Almost a Lynching," "Nearly Mobbed") or as a homicide ("Another Bakota Homicide," "Murder at Deadwood"), and none commented on the mob.
Several printings garbled the names, giving "J. H. Hogan," "I. A. Hogan," "Dan Falney" and "Dan Talvey."

The local account, apparently the Pioneer's own text, treated the shooting as a drunken quarrel, did not mention a mob, and said the paper refrained from "detailed facts or rumors, believing that the laws of the country will be rigidly enforced."
The Press and Daily Dakotaian of Yankton repeated the wire in its Black Hills column and followed the case through Falvey's death and Hogan's trial.
Most reports place the shooting at Central City, and the local account names the Rustic hotel, but a December 1 Dakotaian note says it happened at Golden Gate, with both men "on a drunken spree."
The lynching threat appears only in the wire dispatch and its rewrites; the local account says only that Hogan was captured and placed in custody.

framing.detail: Distant papers ran the Deadwood dispatch under crime headlines such as 'ALMOST A LYNCHING,' 'Nearly Mobbed' and 'Murder at Deadwood,' with no comment on the mob.
The local account treated the shooting as a drunken quarrel, omitted the mob, and said the paper refrained from rumors, 'believing that the laws of the country will be rigidly enforced.'
